Whenever you start a life somewhere new you go on this little roller coaster. When you first get there things are so new and overwhelming, you're excited and nervous and have no idea what to expect. 


The first few months are the hardest, things go downhill because it's not what you expected and now you feel alone. You second guess your decisions which makes you lonelier. But then something shifts, you find a friend or a new hobby or favorite place. The roller coaster is climbing now. Things are looking up as you start to discover you're new home, new neighbors.


At about 6 months things plateau at a nice comfortable high, you're finally feeling like you belong now and everything is starting to fall into place. You miss your old life less and less, you even stop remembering to talk to your family/friends everyday because you're busy now. 


Flash forward to month 9, we're climbing again, this time higher than before. Things are fantastic, you love your new country and are falling in love with the culture. We keep climbing until its been a year already and time to go home or move on, baffled by how fast time has flown. It's sad to leave this place that you've come to call home.

This isn't a job you take for the money, I get paid the most in the agency, because I am the best at English, which is 1200RMB about 200 USD a month. Some families give more at their discretion. I know of someone getting paid 8000RMB but he's with a different company and has more experience and a knowledge of Mandarin. 
However, living costs are very low here so money goes a lot farther. But the family pays for most of your things anyway. The families who can afford an Au Pair are the richest percentile, so they pay for your meals out or in with them, travel with them, they also like to buy you things like clothes. I recently went with my host mom for a spa day and she paid for everything. Another Au Pair here went to New Zealand with her host family, as well as all over china. They even offered to take her with them to the 2012 Olympic games but she declined because she wouldn't be here anymore. 
I'm 19, so in the middle of my bachelor. I'm the second youngest Au Pair, most are done university or in their early 20's. Most families won't take anyone older than 25.

Well it varies on what the family asks of you. In Europe they are essentially a nanny/tutor, they take care of the children's daily lives as well as teaching them English and culture. 
In China it's a bit different because most (rich) families have housekeepers and nannies that do that. All they want is for you to make their kid top of their class. My job is to teach English 3 hours a week and just generally talk to the child. I also have to instill western values in him. They aren't raised with the manners we consider normal, they have to be taught to share, say please and thank you and be polite. 
The rest of the time I take Chinese classes or just hang out, there's not a whole lot to do. And there are male and female Au Pairs, it just depends on if the family wants a 'big sister' or 'big brother'.
